newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon forms task force to review co-ed training.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon forms task force to review co-ed training.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen Friday created a task force to review whether men and women should receive military training together, a practice that came under fire in the aftermath of recent sex scandals.

The 10-member panel, chaired by former Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker, will have six months to make recommendations on a range of training and discipline policies, including the contentious issue of whether the Army, Air Force and Navy should require separate training for men and women.

The military has been bedevilled recently by scandals involving adultery and sexual harassment. Four trainers at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland were charged with sexual misconduct including rape, and one was convicted of rape.

And one of the Pentagon's top candidates to take over as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff recently withdrew his name from consideration amid a highly publicised scandal involving an adulterous affair 13 years ago.
"The problems of Aberdeen and elsewhere have raised questions," Cohen said at a news conference announcing the formation of the special panel.

But Cohen maintained that the review of training practices was not meant to "turn back the clock" for women, who now represent about 14 percent of the nation's military compared to only 2 percent 25 years ago.
"It should be clear to everyone that we cannot run our all-volunteer military effectively without women," he said.

He said the panel will look both at whether men and women should still be trained together as recruits as well as at later stages, noting that problems in Aberdeen involved advanced training programmes.
He said he found "no compelling reason" to change the current status after visiting various military bases. But, he added: "Obviously it's something we still have to look at."
The Marine Corps separates entry-level recruits, then gradually integrates men and women in squads, while the other branches train male and female recruits together.
The panel will also assess the adequacy of current standards aimed at getting recruits into good physical shape once they enter the armed forces.
Cohen said he will use the panel's findings when he makes recommendations to Congress next year on whether changes are needed.
Members of Congress have sharply divided views on whether to train men and women together.
West Virginia Democrat Robert Byrd had raised the prospect of legislation requiring separate military training, but he instead pushed the idea of an independent panel to study the issue.
Task force members include retired military officers and private citizens with expertise in military and civil rights matters.
